1:
Everything turns on who the ruler of the land is, and whether the advice is meant. John Gill takes the lamb as tribute, following a paraphrase, and rehearses the history: Moab was made tributary by David and paid in lambs until the revolt under Ahab, and is now bid to pay the rightful heir in Judah—though he admits the phrase may be rendered as an address, send ye the lamb, O ruler of the land, or as the lamb belonging to that ruler. Charles Ellicott adds that the tribute ceased at a revolt recorded on the Moabite stone, and that the renewal is demanded not for the northern kingdom, then on the point of extinction, but for the king of Judah as the true ruler; he takes the naming of the rock either as the city later known by its Greek name or as the rock-country generally, and infers that the invaders had made the northern fords impassable, so the tribute must go south; he wonders too whether the words summon Edom to a like submission. Matthew Henry agrees it is tribute, levied from one frontier to the other and sent to the city of David, and notices that some read instead a lamb for sacrifice to the ruler of the whole earth, and some take even that ironically, as upbraiding a people who delayed repenting. He rejects the irony, taking it as good advice seriously given, of a piece with the prophet who told a king to break off his sins by righteousness if it might lengthen his tranquillity.

John Calvin takes the opposite of nearly all of this. He rejects the reading of an early Latin father, adopted he says by almost all Christians, which referred the lamb to Christ as descended through a Moabite ancestress, and calls it so destitute of plausibility that it need not be refuted. He rejects the Jewish reading of tribute more sharply, since we nowhere read that Moab was tributary to Judah, and the passage cited in support concerns the northern kingdom. So the ruler is God himself, the land the whole earth, the lamb a sacrifice, and the whole spoken in irony: a condemnation of late repentance, telling them they will attempt in vain what they might once have done easily and to their profit. John Wesley takes the sacrifice reading without the irony, counselling them to make peace with God by sacrifice for the injuries done to him and his people, and identifying the mount as the temple. Adam Clarke alone works the text. The versions divide between I will send, send thou and send ye, and one of them with five manuscripts reads a son rather than a lamb, which would make these verses describe the prince’s son fleeing through the desert; but he concludes there is perhaps less difficulty here than appears, and falls back on tribute paid as formerly, that the punishment might be mitigated.

The fluttering birds are agreed in sense but disputed in force. Ellicott prefers a forsaken nest to a bird cast out of one, allows the daughters of Moab to mean either the women driven from their homes or the whole population, and pictures them uncertain whether to return home or cross into a strange land, comparing a Greek tragedian. Keil and Delitzsch read the verse as showing the advice taken, and eagerly; the people were already birds soaring about in their flight, but the simile describes the state the counsel throws them into, an anxious indecision like birds driven from a nest that wheel round and dare not return. Calvin, having made the advice ironic, makes the metaphor one of terror only, so that they flee at the rustling of a leaf—the trembling and wearisome flight of a people who had abused their tranquillity. Gill supplies the connection the others leave implicit: this is what follows if the tribute is not paid.
3:
The direction of the plea splits them evenly. Keil and Delitzsch have Moab speaking: the humbled people stand at the far border of what was once their land and address these petitions to Zion, placing their fate in the hands of the men of Judah, and asking at noon for Zion’s shade as for the blackness of night. Charles Ellicott agrees the verse is spoken not by the prophet to Moab but by Moab to the rulers of Judah, who are asked to be as the shadow of a great rock in a weary land—though he records critics who keep the prophet as speaker and make it a call on Moab to shelter fugitives. Adam Clarke settles it from grammar: the verbs are singular and feminine, agreeing with Zion, and on the next verse he holds that let the outcasts of Moab sojourn with thee, O Zion, is much the most obvious construction, confirmed by the Greek and Syriac. Ellicott renders it the same way, Judah being safe herself and appealed to for mercy on Moabite fugitives. The others read it the other way about. John Gill has the king of Moab consulting his nobles about harbouring the Jews; John Calvin pictures God himself performing the part of a suppliant, pleading as a neighbour and kinsman—receive those in distress, and if you will not assist them at least do them no harm.

Calvin carries forward the irony of the opening verse. The Moabites had overturned counsel and judgment by fraud while power was theirs, and are advised to execute the very justice they destroyed at the moment all authority has been stripped from them—an upbraiding he compares to the taunt addressed to Adam. From the same verse he draws the opposite lesson: God takes injuries done to his people as done to himself, and nothing is more acceptable than kindness to fugitives, or more abominable than cruelty. John Wesley makes the outcasts God’s own people driven from their land, whom he owns though he has chastened them, and reads the promised end of the oppressor as meaning the kindness will not go unrewarded; Clarke guesses that oppressor was the northern kingdom which once invaded Judah.

The throne divides them again. Gill takes it of Hezekiah, whose government was settled after the overthrow of the Assyrian army, allowing that he was a type and the ultimate view may be Christ’s kingdom. Clarke asks whether it may not refer to that king and makes the verse a portrait of the ruler who cannot fail to be a blessing: he sits in truth and is not merely called father of his people; he is judging, not a man of war wasting his subjects’ lives to satisfy ambition; he seeks judgment, hunting out the poor who cannot come to him; and he hastens righteousness, allowing no court to delay a cause—delays answering little end, he adds, but the enriching of unprincipled lawyers. Ellicott renders it less definitely, that in mercy a throne shall be established and one sit on it in truth, thinking of the ideal king of the earlier chapters, of whom Hezekiah was a partial type. Calvin denies the Jewish reading flatly: it is altogether inappropriate to Hezekiah, since a greater restoration is in view and Moab was not punished while his reign flourished, so the verse can be explained of none but Christ, though Hezekiah was his type. He presses the mercy as the sole cause, no excellence of character having moved God to raise a throne fallen through the crimes of the people, and makes something of the humble word tabernacle: this kingdom does not shine with gold or precious stones, and its mean shape shows that Christ reigns among men, so we need not go to heaven to seek him. Wesley reads the same word historically, David’s house being then more a tent than a strong palace.
6:
Matthew Henry reads the turn as the prophet checking himself: having given good counsel he despairs of its being taken, for those who will not be counselled cannot be helped: he would have healed them, but they would not be healed. He makes pride the chief charge, thinking more precious souls ruined by it than by any one lust; the Moabites forget the baseness of their origin, and this is the character all who know them give. Being proud they will not be advised, and scorn to take a righteous king for a pattern, supposing themselves able to teach him. Wrath follows, since the very proud are commonly very passionate. John Calvin works the same words harder. He takes the verse as anticipation, the Moabites being then flourishing and their haughtiness a powerful weapon for shaking the minds of the Jews, and prefers to render the second noun not wrath but outrage, from a root meaning to pass over: those who claim more than is due kindle at the smallest offence, being not only passionate but outrageous, wishing all to yield to them and themselves to none—while the humble forgive an injury easily. John Gill and John Wesley keep it short, Gill with the maxim that pride comes before a fall, Wesley that the prophet turns from Moab to God’s people because he expects his counsel to do no good.

The closing clause is disputed. Charles Ellicott renders it that the boasts are of no worth, not so as they seem. Calvin notes that the word rendered lies may mean lies, boasting or divinations, that the Greek translators took it the last way, and that he prefers boastings; on the phrase not so he declines the senses not right and not true for a negative confirmation, that there will be no firmness in these counsels. Henry records a rendering that turns the verse into a comparison, the haughtiness and pride and wrath being greater than the strength, so that Moab has not power equal to his malice. Adam Clarke emends one word from two manuscripts and the parallel prophecy, and fills his space with another prophet’s threat that a people who magnified themselves against God’s borders would become a desolation for ever.

The wailing that follows is agreed in substance. Gill hears one Moabite mourning for another, the living for the dead, or one part of the country answering another in turns; Henry has every one howling in despair, none able to see cause or find heart to encourage his friend. Calvin calls it a melancholy concert in which they complain to each other, and rejects the rendering that limits the howling, since what follows makes it universal. Its object is not. Keil and Delitzsch observe that the fortress was already destroyed, so the word must mean the strong foundations laid bare, that is, ruins—while conceding that in every other passage it means a kind of grape-cake. Ellicott gives that alternative full weight, since the word does elsewhere mean raisin-cakes, which may have been the town’s chief product, the traffic in it lost with the vineyards; Ruins, he concludes, would in any case be better than foundations. Clarke calls the received reading a palpable mistake happily corrected by the parallel prophecy, which reads not foundations or flagons but men, so the mourning is for the men of the city; and the name, he insists, is the shorter form. Calvin keeps foundations and finds a reason for them: the prophet names these rather than the city because nothing is to be left of it, so they mourn not a plundering but an entire overthrow. On the last word he sets aside the reading that makes it hired mourning, taking it to mean that all who are left will be wounded, not one safe. Wesley adds only that this city survived when the others fell, so its ruin was the more lamented.
8:
The clause about the lords of the heathen is read two ways. Charles Ellicott allows the received rendering, that they broke down the principal plants, but reports that most recent critics prefer another equally admissible—that the branches smote down the lords of the nations, the wine being so strong it overcame the princes who drank it. Adam Clarke presses the same view: the wines were in high repute with the great men of neighbouring countries, who indulged in them to intemperance, and the verb means knocked down, that is, overpowered and intoxicated. The others keep the destroyers. John Wesley names them the great rulers of the eastern nations, and takes the choicest plants to stand not for the fruits only but for the choicest people; John Calvin has the vines torn out by conquerors who had subdued the nations in war.

The reach of the vineyards is disputed on the same principle. Ellicott says the pronoun may refer either to the branches or to the lords as destroyers, and adopting the first finds a description of how far the culture extended, north to the Gilead frontier, east into the wilderness, and west across the Dead Sea. Calvin knows the reading that refers it to the enemies and would rather supply a relative and refer it to the vineyards, so that though they covered so large a tract, all will be trodden down; he takes the crossing of the sea as the practice of embanking good soil against the waves. Wesley refers it the other way, the lords coming as far as the utmost border, and reads the stretched-out branches as people driven from their homes and dispersed. John Gill keeps to the fields, languishing through drought, or forage, or treading, or because no men were left to till them.

Who weeps in the next verse is a real division. Keil and Delitzsch make the tears the prophet’s own and justify them: the beauty and fruitfulness of a land are gifts from the riches of divine goodness, remnants of the paradisaical beginning of human history, so no matter of indifference to the spirit of prophecy, and it is not unworthy of a prophet who predicts the renewal of nature to weep over such a devastation. Ellicott says the same briefly, that he will weep with tears as genuine as the town’s own. Calvin denies it. The prophet takes on the character of another and laments in the name of the Moabites, representing as on a stage the grief that will be felt after the calamity, to give weight to the instruction—though he grants that believers do shudder at God’s judgments and cannot lay aside human feeling so far as not to pity the wicked in their destruction. Gill connects the mourning for vines with a people he calls given to drink.

The shout at the end divides them again. Ellicott renders it that a shout is fallen upon the summer fruits and harvest, meaning not the song of the vintagers but the cry of the enemy trampling the fields, the contrast sharpened by using the very word that serves in the next verse for the song of those who tread the grapes. Calvin canvasses the alternatives—that the verb means to fail, or that the sense is that the glad voices of the reapers shall be heard no longer—and prefers the enemy’s shout, following the parallel prophecy as the most faithful interpreter: when thou preparest to gather harvest and vintage the enemy will break in, and instead of a cheerful song his shout will drive thee away. Wesley keeps the reading Calvin sets aside, that the joyful shouts customary at harvest and vintage cease. Clarke finds two great mistakes here which the parallel text rectifies: harvest should be vintage, these places never having been celebrated for a harvest, and the shouting should be the destroyer, who has fallen upon it.
10:
The silencing of the vintage songs is described alike by all. John Calvin notes the custom ended, that those who gathered the grapes testified their joy by dancing and singing; John Wesley that the juice was squeezed out by treading with the feet; John Gill that gladness is gathered in though the harvest was not. Keil and Delitzsch remark that the word rendered plentiful field is one of the prophet’s favourites, serving both as place-name and as common noun, and that with this verse he is plunged deeper into mourning. But the closing clause raises the question governing what follows. Charles Ellicott takes it as spoken by God, declaring the desolation, though wrought by human hands, to be his, so that the prophet, while he weeps in true human pity, is taught not to forget that it is a righteous punishment. Keil and Delitzsch agree, and infer that the harp-like sounding of the bowels in the next verse might then be the feelings of God, the Scriptures not hesitating to ascribe such feelings to him. Adam Clarke denies it flatly: the Greek read the verb as a passive third person, and rightly, for God is not the speaker here.

On the harp the readings diverge again along the same line. Ellicott concedes the context leaves it uncertain whether the prophet or God speaks, thinks the prophet more natural, and observes that the very phrase is used elsewhere of divine compassion; Gill has the harp sounding when stricken, as here by the punitive hand of God, but assigns the words to the Moabites themselves, the survivors lamenting their country, the prophet putting it so to show that if it pained him it must pain them more. Calvin says the same in his own terms: the prophet assumes the character of a Moabite and describes a grief so intense the bowels make a distressing noise, such lively description serving to set the event before our eyes and strengthen hope in what seems past belief. Wesley keeps it simple: in excessive grief the bowels are rolled together so as to make an audible noise—the bowels standing where we now put the heart—and the feeling is compassion.

The last verse turns on a weariness. Gill takes it of wearying themselves with weeping, or with heaping up sacrifices and going from one high place to another as an early king of that people did, so that when it appears the crying was in vain they will be ashamed and try another method; a Jewish interpreter, he notes, makes them instead weary of fighting on the high places of their towers. Ellicott renders it as one sentence—when Moab appears as a worshipper, when he wearies himself on the high place, though he enter the sanctuary to pray, yet shall he not prevail—and calls it a picture of unavailing litanies, comparing the prophets of Baal, as Keil and Delitzsch do; they add that the word for appearing is carried over from Israelite worship into a heathen setting, the two verbs forming a pictorial assonance the prophet delights in. Clarke suspects the two are variant readings of each other, a very probable conjecture. Calvin refuses the reading that makes the failure physical, that they shall be too worn out to reach the temple, and takes it as shutting them out from all hope, since they will find no protection even in their gods. He presses the word seen: idolaters are guided not by reason but by what strikes their senses, crediting their superstitions when they succeed and cursing their gods when they fail. He observes that men in calamity leave the nearest place of worship for a more famous one at a distance, expecting to be better heard, and concludes that this people will enter that temple at last more from shame than judgment. Wesley ends it in a line: their god can neither hear nor help.
13:
The closing formula is taken by most as a seal on what precedes. John Gill says it comes from the Lord and is the word of God and not of man, so shall certainly come to pass; John Calvin calls the sentence a ratification, in which the prophet lays aside the person of a man and introduces God speaking; Keil and Delitzsch describe the burden as closed and an epilogue following, which fixes the term of a fulfilment for something not now predicted for the first time. John Wesley reads the phrase as covering the span since God first began to reveal this matter to him. Charles Ellicott alone draws a conclusion about authorship. The phrase, he says, is used of an indefinite past, like our of yore, and is elsewhere rendered hitherto and from the beginning; it seems to imply that thus far the prophet had been in part reproducing an older prophet’s burden, or one given him to deliver at an earlier date.

All then mark a sharp change of manner. Gill treats what follows as a distinct prophecy with a date annexed: the earlier concerns the utter destruction of Moab by the Babylonians, of which a later prophet writes in much the same language, while this is a lesser blow to come shortly, by one or another of the Assyrian kings. Ellicott finds the contrast in exactly that, the vaguer character of what precedes against the dated prediction that follows. Wesley agrees the three years point to a great blow from which the nation recovered and flourished again until a later conqueror completed its ruin. Adam Clarke adds that the conqueror of that day left men in the land, the final desolation being reserved for another.

The measure of the term is worked hard. Ellicott explains that the years are measured with the exactness of the hired labourer who will not give more than he contracted for, and the employer who will not take less. Keil and Delitzsch put it as a rule: of working time the hirer remits nothing and the labourer gives nothing in, so the statement is exact—three years, rather under than over. Clarke sharpens it, that as the hireling counts to a single day and will not stay an hour beyond his agreement, so destruction will come in three years even to a day. But Clarke reports the variant that would blunt this: nine manuscripts and two old editions read about three years, which he says leaves the prophecy not so definite, though he judges the received text may well stand. Calvin gives the fixing of a term a pastoral purpose: not for certainty only but so believers may not faint through longer delay; and he presses the comparison the others leave flat, that hirelings long for the appointed day of their reward because they groan under the burden and dislike their toil.

On the outcome there is a last divergence. Calvin notes that the great multitude is expressly mentioned because their number was large and they boasted of it and thought themselves invincible, so the change will leave nothing resembling their former condition, nothing but a sad and shocking sight; Wesley makes the glory their strength and wealth and whatever else they gloried in, now contemptible to those who once admired it. Keil and Delitzsch observe that only a remnant is left, a contemptible one, and add that every history of the nations is but the shadow of the history of Israel. Ellicott presses the same word the other way: here too a remnant, but not like Israel’s, the germ of a renewed strength. He also grants what none of the others admit, that history is silent as to the manner of the fulfilment, inferring only that men must have looked on it as an instance of the writer’s foresight, since it was preserved when his writings were collected.
